title: The issue with HIT (the intensity meme)
summary: NH attacks High Intensity Training as preached online (one hard set, 20-minute workouts, low frequency, deload weeks), using a poster called 'American Ubermensch' as a foil. He argues intensity is essential but can't be separated from volume and frequency, that HIT icons Mentzer and Yates were enhanced, and that a good program should give naturals a PR nearly every session.
claims: Programming concepts get bent over time to sell products or to make theory fit someone's practice
Intensity is the effort a lift demands relative to your max; 100% is your best effort, usually calculated from a 1RM, though 10RMs can work
Shouting, forced failure, partials or chains don't change what intensity is; they are jargon and sometimes misapplications, less effective than straight RPE work
Proper high-intensity training means pushing intensity to progress in strength and tonnage over time; percentages around 90-95% are fine, but 100%+ is unnecessary and dangerous for bodybuilding
Anyone saying you can grow on volume and pump alone is on PEDs or looks like they don't lift
A method working for you doesn't prove it is superior; novices grow on anything new, as long as they're in a caloric surplus
Followers of a method are often attached to the person promoting it, not to the method, and stay attached even if the creator later recants
Naturals can't base training on enhanced lifters like Mentzer and Yates; steroid users grow regardless of style, as the variety of pro training shows
When people use smugness, jokes or personal attacks to promote a training principle, the principle is usually garbage
'Training hard' is relative to work capacity: for NH two hours with high-intensity windows is hard, one hour isn't, and going beyond his maximum recoverable volume is overtraining
Don't compare how hard you work with others; grimacing and screaming aren't hard training; hard training is planned on paper and produces progress
Muscles aren't only for brief efforts; farmers who work all day at submaximal loads become strong and bulky, because using muscle makes it grow
Training to failure means stopping short of failure; failing reps signals a programming problem
Forced reps and forced negatives only extend a set that should already be over; they add a little intensity but nothing magical
Doing one hard set of bench and one of squat in a session wastes time because each lift needs its own long warm-up
NH isn't a fan of full-body programs: they can work done properly, but most people mess them up
Trembling, flu-like symptoms or soreness aren't signs of growth; the best indicators are strength progression and tonnage over time
Still getting DOMS after six months on the same program and lifts means your frequency is too low and the body unlearns how to recover between sessions
Intensity, volume and frequency are linked: adding a rep to a single hard set raises volume, so raising intensity requires raising volume and frequency too
Recovery is like a bathtub of fixed size: if legs recover in two days, train them again after two days; training once a week doesn't make the tub bigger
Training a body part only once a week is always suboptimal unless you're deliberately sandbagging
NH's warm-ups alone take at least 30 minutes; 20-minute workouts are only for complete novices with zero work capacity
One hard set, twice a week, 20 minutes, no accessories can't make naturals grow; those who grew on such protocols were enhanced
Muscles recover between sets just as between sessions, so a second set (e.g. 8 then 7 reps) adds more fibre damage and growth
Deload weeks are useless for bodybuilders unless injured
With the right rep range and program you should hit a PR every time you train a lift; otherwise you're sandbagging, which should only be deliberate
NH says he has progressed on every filmed lift without interruption, adding a rep every session
